title: Tympanoplasty type 1 (underlay)
subtitle: Freshen the edge, see the chain, graft medial to the remnant

sources.title: Theory and practice of tympanoplasty (Wullstein H)

sources.org: European Academy of Otology and Neurotology and Japan Otological Society (EAONO/JOS)
sources.title: EAONO/JOS joint consensus statements on the definitions, classification and staging of middle ear cholesteatoma (Yung M et al., J Int Adv Otol)

indications: A persistent dry tympanic membrane perforation (chronic otitis media without cholesteatoma) causing conductive hearing loss, recurrent discharge with water exposure, or both.

Type 1 tympanoplasty in Wullstein's classification: repair of the drum with an intact, mobile ossicular chain. If the chain is not intact, the operation becomes an ossiculoplasty or a staged procedure.
Traumatic perforations that have not healed after an adequate period of observation.
Closure of a perforation to allow a hearing aid to be worn without recurrent infection.
contraindications: Cholesteatoma, which needs a different operation. Look for retraction pockets, debris and attic erosion before listing.
Active discharge on the day of surgery is a relative contraindication. Many surgeons expect a dry ear for a period before grafting; treat infection first.
An only hearing ear, or the better hearing ear, is a relative contraindication: the small risk of sensorineural loss weighs more heavily.
Uncontrolled Eustachian tube dysfunction, cleft palate or active sinonasal disease, which predict graft failure; treat or accept the higher failure rate with the patient informed.
preparation: Pure tone audiogram with masking within an agreed interval. A conductive loss much larger than the perforation size explains suggests ossicular discontinuity or fixation, and the consent should cover it.
Microscopic examination in clinic to confirm the margins of the perforation are visible, the remnant is healthy, and there is no cholesteatoma or squamous ingrowth.
Decide the approach in advance: permeatal or endoscopic for small posterior perforations with a wide canal, endaural or postaural for anterior, subtotal or poorly visible perforations.

Consent risks to discuss: graft failure and residual perforation, hearing that is unchanged or worse including a small risk of a dead ear, tinnitus, dizziness, taste change from chorda tympani stretch or division, facial nerve injury (rare), numb pinna, wound problems and canal stenosis.
Tell the patient they will need to keep the ear dry and avoid nose blowing and flying for a period that the surgeon will specify.
positioning: Supine with the head turned away from the operative ear on a head ring, with head-up tilt.
Table rotated so the surgeon's line of sight runs down the canal; the head is not moved during the operation.
Pressure care and eye protection, and the tube fixed on the non-operative side.
equipment: Operating microscope with an otological objective, or a rigid endoscope for an endoscopic approach.
Ear specula, speculum holder, otological microinstruments: Rosen needle, round knife, sickle knife, Plester elevator, cupped forceps, Bellucci scissors and fine suckers.
Otological drill with small diamond burrs for canalplasty if the anterior canal wall bulges.
Fascia press, gelatin sponge, and the chosen graft material (temporalis fascia, perichondrium or cartilage). Ear pack per surgeon practice.
anatomy: The tympanic membrane has a pars tensa held in the tympanic sulcus by the fibrous annulus, and a pars flaccida above the lateral process of the malleus. The handle of the malleus is embedded in the pars tensa.
The tympanomeatal flap is posterior canal skin raised together with the posterior annulus, giving entry to the middle ear behind the drum.
Behind the posterosuperior quadrant lie the long process of the incus, the incudostapedial joint, the stapes and the chorda tympani running across the medial surface of the drum.
The facial nerve runs above the oval window in the tympanic segment, where its bony canal is often dehiscent.
The Eustachian tube opens anteriorly in the protympanum. An anterior perforation is harder to graft because the anterior canal wall often hides its edge and the graft has less support.
criticalSafety: See the whole perforation edge before grafting. A bulging anterior canal wall that hides the anterior margin needs a canalplasty, not a guess.
Remove the squamous epithelium from the perforation rim and the undersurface of the remnant, or it will grow inwards and form a cholesteatoma pearl behind the graft.
Handle the ossicles only to test them. Do not move the chain vigorously; trauma to the stapes can damage the inner ear.
If cholesteatoma is found, stop treating this as a tympanoplasty: follow the bail-out step.
structuresAtRisk: Jugular bulb in the hypotympanum (rarely high and dehiscent)
commonErrors: Grafting a perforation whose anterior edge was never seen.
Leaving epithelium on the inner surface of the remnant.
A tympanomeatal flap that is torn or too short, leaving bare bone that granulates.
Too little support for the graft anteriorly, so it falls medially away from the remnant and the perforation recurs.
complications: Graft failure with a residual perforation.
Conductive loss that persists from unrecognised ossicular disease, sensorineural hearing loss including a dead ear, tinnitus and vertigo.
Taste disturbance from chorda tympani injury, usually temporary.
Epithelial pearl or iatrogenic cholesteatoma, blunting or lateralisation of the graft, canal stenosis, wound infection and facial nerve injury (rare).
postop: Head bandage overnight if a postaural incision was used. Ear pack per surgeon practice, usually removed in clinic after one to three weeks.
Keep the ear dry, no nose blowing, sneeze with the mouth open, and avoid flying and heavy straining until the surgeon advises.
Document facial function and check for vertigo and nystagmus in recovery. Persistent vertigo or a sudden drop in hearing needs same-day review.
A post-operative audiogram once the graft has healed, usually after a few months, to compare with the baseline.

steps.emphasis: Consent covers ossicular reconstruction or staging if the chain is found to be abnormal, and conversion if cholesteatoma is found.
Audiogram on display: side, the size of the air-bone gap, and the bone conduction in the operated ear.
Antibiotic prophylaxis per local policy; it is not routinely required for a clean, dry ear.
Laryngeal mask or tube by agreement; a smooth emergence without coughing protects the graft.
Head turned away with head-up tilt; the table, not the head, is rotated during the case.
Infiltrate the canal skin slowly at four quadrants, watching it blanch without blebbing, and the postaural sulcus if that approach is used.
For a permeatal or endoscopic approach, harvest fascia or tragal perichondrium through a small separate incision instead.
Only if needed: a canalplasty of the anterior canal wall bulge, with the canal skin protected and the burr kept off the drum remnant and malleus.
Bipolar to the postaural wound only. In the canal, control is with adrenaline cottonoids and patience.
Layered closure of the postaural wound and a mastoid head bandage.
Count cottonoids, including the tiny pledgets used in the canal.
Record perforation size and site, the state of the ossicles, the graft and its position, and whether the chorda was preserved.

step.tymp.freshen.title: Freshen the perforation edge
step.tymp.freshen.why: A perforation persists because its edge has healed as a rim of squamous epithelium. Removing that rim gives a raw edge that will grow on to the graft, and removing epithelium from the undersurface prevents a cholesteatoma pearl behind the new drum.
how: With a Rosen needle or sickle knife, incise just outside the epithelial rim all the way round the perforation.
Remove the rim with cupped forceps as a ring, so you can see that it is complete.
Scrape the undersurface of the remnant near the edge with a right-angled pick to remove any inturned epithelium.
Keep the fragments out of the middle ear; remove them with the sucker.
pitfalls: Incomplete freshening anteriorly, where the edge is hard to see.
Pushing epithelial fragments into the middle ear.

step.tymp.flap.title: Raise the tympanomeatal flap and enter the middle ear
step.tymp.flap.why: The flap gives access to the middle ear without enlarging the perforation, and carries the annulus that will hold the graft. The chorda tympani lies immediately behind the posterosuperior annulus.
how: Make two radial canal incisions, roughly at 12 and 6 o'clock positions, joined by a curved incision several millimetres lateral to the annulus.
Elevate the canal skin medially in one sheet with a round knife, keeping the elevator on bone and the bleeding controlled with adrenaline cottonoids.
At the annulus, lift it out of the sulcus posteriorly and enter the middle ear under the mucosa.
Identify the chorda tympani and the long process of the incus before lifting further superiorly. Free the chorda gently rather than dividing it.
pitfalls: Tearing the flap by elevating in more than one direction at a time.
Entering the middle ear above the chorda and stretching or dividing it.

step.tymp.middle-ear.title: Inspect the middle ear and test the ossicular chain
step.tymp.middle-ear.why: A type 1 tympanoplasty only restores hearing if the chain conducts. Finding a fixed stapes, an eroded incus or hidden cholesteatoma now changes the operation; finding it later means another one.
how: Inspect the mucosa, the round window niche, the oval window, the incudostapedial joint and the visible part of the facial canal.
Palpate the malleus handle gently and watch the incus and stapes move; look for the round window reflex as a sign of a mobile chain.
Look for squamous debris, white masses or retraction into the sinus tympani or attic. Use an angled endoscope if the view is limited.
Record the findings aloud so they are in the note.
pitfalls: Moving the malleus vigorously enough to transmit trauma to the stapes.
Grafting over an unrecognised ossicular discontinuity.

step.tymp.cholesteatoma-bailout.title: Bail-out: cholesteatoma or an abnormal chain
step.tymp.cholesteatoma-bailout.why: A tympanoplasty that covers cholesteatoma hides it under a healthy-looking drum until it has eroded further. A chain that does not conduct makes the repair pointless for hearing. Both change the plan and must be named.
how: If cholesteatoma is found, remove it only if it is limited, fully visible and consented for; otherwise stop, close, and plan a properly consented and imaged mastoid operation.
If the incus is eroded or the stapes fixed, perform an ossiculoplasty only if consented and equipped; otherwise graft the drum now and stage the ossicular reconstruction.
Tell the patient after surgery what was found and why the operation was changed or stopped, and record it in the note.
pitfalls: Extending a day-case myringoplasty into a mastoid operation without consent or imaging.
Grafting over residual squamous epithelium to finish the planned operation.

step.tymp.graft.title: Place the underlay graft
step.tymp.graft.why: An underlay graft sits medial to the drum remnant, supported from below, so the remnant's raw edge grows across it. Its success depends on contact with the remnant all the way round, especially anteriorly, and on support that keeps it there.
how: Fill the middle ear, particularly anteriorly towards the Eustachian tube, with gelatin sponge to support the graft.
Trim the dried fascia so it overlaps the perforation edge generously on all sides.
Slide the graft under the remnant and, according to technique, under or over the handle of the malleus, and tuck it anteriorly under the anterior remnant so it cannot fall medially.
Check through the perforation that the graft is in contact with the whole rim and that no gap remains anteriorly.
pitfalls: Too little anterior support, so the graft drops away from the anterior edge.
A graft that is too small, discovered when it is already wet and floppy.

step.tymp.flap-replace.title: Replace the flap and pack the canal
step.tymp.flap-replace.why: The tympanomeatal flap holds the posterior graft edge in place and covers bare bone. A canal pack keeps everything in position while it adheres.
how: Lay the tympanomeatal flap back over the posterior edge of the graft, with the annulus in the sulcus and the canal skin flat on bone.
Place gelatin sponge in the canal against the drum and flap to hold them.
Insert the outer canal pack per surgeon practice, avoiding pressure that could displace the graft.
pitfalls: A rolled flap edge left over the graft, causing blunting or a pearl.
A tight pack that lateralises the graft.
